extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotle; readers/students of virtue ethics and classical moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and systematizing Aristotle's evaluative principles about Pleasure and Happiness (chief good, nature of pleasure, and the contemplative life) as presented in the Nicomachean Ethics excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as candidate for the Chief Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Eudoxus's position: Pleasure is the Chief Good because all (rational and irrational) aim at it; what all aim at must be good and the best; pleasure is chosen for its own sake and makes other goods more choice-worthy when added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as a theory to be tested: does universal aiming at something prove it best? Consider objections (e.g., combination with practical wisdom, mixed vs. unmixed pleasures) and whether being chosen for itself suffices to make something the Chief Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good must be final and self-sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good (Happiness) must be chosen for its own sake (not for something further) and be self-sufficient; it is an End that comprehends other ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion to evaluate candidate chief goods: reject things sought for other ends (e.g., rest, amusements) and require that the candidate leave nothing lacking to make life complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is an activity (Working) in accordance with Excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is not a mere state but a kind of activity — specifically activity in accordance with virtue/excellence; actions done in accordance with Virtue are choice-worthy for their own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess lives by looking at sustained activities (workings) expressing excellence rather than passive states; prefer enduring, noble activities over mere amusement or rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemplative life as highest happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The activity of the Intellect (contemplation) is the highest form of Happiness because the Intellect is the supreme internal principle, its activity is most continuous, self-sufficient, pleasant in a pure and permanent way, and requires fewer external goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ranking lives, give priority to contemplative/scientific activity: evaluate continuity, self-sufficiency, purity of pleasure, and the degree to which the activity is an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure perfects working
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure accompanies and perfects every percipient faculty’s working: the best and most pleasant is the working of the best faculty on the best object within its range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge pleasures by whether they arise from excellent exercise of faculties on fitting objects; prefer pleasures that enhance accuracy, endurance, and perfection of activity (e.g., the pleasure of the geometrician in geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is a whole, not a Movement or Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is complete at any moment (like an act of sight) and is not a movement or generation, which are processes extended in time and divisible into parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pleasures that are instantaneous-whole from processes; do not conflate pleasure with change or becoming when assessing its nature and fitness as a chief good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures differ in kind according to faculties and workings
rubrics_metrics.description: Different faculties (sight, hearing, intellect, etc.) have distinct pleasures proper to their workings; likewise different animals and characters have pleasures proper to their natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pleasures contextually: identify the faculty/activity they perfect and recognize that pleasures are not homogeneous — compare like with like (intellectual vs. sensual pleasures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper pleasures aid their workings; foreign pleasures hinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures proper to a working increase its accuracy and endurance, while pleasures foreign to that working interfere with or destroy it (analogous to pains proper to a working).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer pleasures that are intrinsic to and supportive of valuable activities; treat pleasures that repeatedly distract from or undermine important activities as detrimental to flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all apparent pleasures are real pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures derived from disgraceful or depraved tastes are not truly pleasures in the relevant moral sense (they are pleasant only to the ill-disposed), analogous to how diseased palates misperceive tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize the source and moral quality of pleasures: pleasures that depend on vicious dispositions or corrupt perceptions should be discounted when identifying genuine goods for human flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not merely supply after lack
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is not simply the supply of something previously lacking (as in bodily nourishment); many pleasures (mathematical, certain sensory pleasures) occur without any prior pain or lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing pleasure to relief from pain; recognize pleasures that arise from exercise or appreciation without preceding deprivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and limit do not exclude a pleasure from being good
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection: pleasure is unlimited/admitting degrees; Aristotle’s response: many goods (health, virtues) admit degrees and can still be limited; unmixed vs. mixed pleasures explain apparent unlimitedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether pleasure can be a chief good, account for gradations and mixtures rather than dismissing pleasures on grounds of degree/limitability alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: The good man as measure of real pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: What impresses the good man as pleasant is to be counted real pleasure; the virtuous person's perception helps measure which pleasures are genuinely choice-worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the judgments of the virtuous (the good man) as a normative touchstone: privileges pleasures that accord with virtue and reject those that the good man would not endorse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness requires complete life/duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Happiness requires a complete duration of life; happiness should be judged over a full life-span, since some points of happiness are incomplete without sufficient time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a life’s happiness over its entire duration rather than isolated episodes; partial or interrupted lives cannot be straightforwardly judged as fully happy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical virtues depend more on external goods than contemplative life
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical moral virtues (liberality, justice, bravery, self-mastery) often require external conditions and goods (money, opportunities, power) to manifest, whereas contemplative activity needs these less and sometimes is hindered by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing kinds of Happiness, factor in the external goods necessary for the exercise of different virtues; the contemplative life scores higher for self-sufficiency and minimal external dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is not mere amusement or rest
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness cannot be amusement or rest (ends chosen for leisure alone); amusement is an accompaniment or rest but not the final End toward which one should toil all life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject candidates for the good that are merely forms of amusement or rest; prefer activities that are earnest, serious, and choice-worthy for their own sakes.
